title: Prompt Engineering
oneLiner: How you ask changes what you get: clear roles, instructions, examples and formats make answers reliable, and tools and format rules make them usable by software.

what.html:
Prompt engineering is designing the text you give a model so it does the job well, without any training. A good prompt has a role, a clear instruction, the needed context, a few examples, and an output format. On top of that come techniques: asking several times and voting (self-consistency), splitting work into steps (chaining), letting the model call tools, and forcing structured output.

Everyday versionBriefing a new colleague: tell them their role, the task, background facts, show two finished examples, and say exactly how you want the result handed back. Vague briefs get vague work.

why.html:
• It's the fastest, cheapest way to adapt a model.
  • Apps need answers in exact formats they can parse.
  • Tool calling is the first step toward agents.

how.title: Five ingredients
how.html: Role, instruction, context, examples, output format. Leave one out and the model has to guess.

how.title: Show, don't just tell
how.html: Zero-shot gives only the instruction; few-shot adds solved examples. The model learns the pattern from the prompt itself, no retraining.

how.title: Be specific
how.html: Say who it's for, how long, what tone, and what a good answer includes. Put instructions before the data and fence the data off.

how.title: Ask several times, then vote
how.html: If one answer is right 60% of the time, the majority of 21 answers is right about 83% of the time. More samples, more cost.

how.title: Automate and chain
how.html: Let a model propose and test prompt wordings, and split big jobs into steps: extract → filter → summarise.

how.title: Let the model call tools
how.html: The model writes a structured request like get_weather(city = Pune); your code checks and runs it and hands back the result.

how.title: Force the format
how.html: Block every word that would break the required format, so the output always parses. It guarantees shape, not truth.

example.html:
Voting. Four sampled answers: 42, 42, 7, 42. The majority is 42 (3 of 4), so that's the final answer, even though one path went wrong.

Supplementary Small changes in wording or example order can change results noticeably, so test prompts on a set of cases, not just one.

takeaways: Role, instruction, context, examples, output format.
Zero-shot vs few-shot; ICL learns from the prompt.
Self-consistency: majority vote helps when p > 0.5.
Chaining, function calling and constrained decoding make outputs usable.
thirty: Prompt engineering adapts models without training. Components: role, instruction, context, examples, output format. Zero-shot uses only instructions; few-shot adds k examples; in-context learning infers the task from them (balance and order matter, diminishing returns). Good instructions state audience, length, tone, constraints and success criteria, put instructions before delimited data, and allow 'I don't know'. Self-consistency samples n answers and takes the majority: with p = 0.6 accuracy reaches 0.68 at n = 5 and 0.83 at n = 21. Automatic prompt engineering searches candidate instructions on a validation set; chaining splits tasks into steps (extract → filter → summarise). Function calling: the model emits a schema-conforming call, the app validates and executes it, and the result returns to the model. Constrained decoding masks tokens that break a schema or grammar, guaranteeing valid structure ("42" instead of "forty") but not correctness.
